title: Twenty-Six Pegs
tagline: How pilots, police and call centres learned to spell without mistakes, and how the same twenty-six words can hold a list or a procedure.
card: The radio spelling alphabet as a set of twenty-six pegs for lists and step-by-step procedures.
goal: you will learn the twenty-six code words of the international spelling alphabet, give each a picture, and use them as pegs for a list and for a procedure.

left_off.q: Name the five families of irregular verbs.
left_off.a: I-A-U; -ought/-aught; come; -ow/-ew/-own; and the odd ones (go, be, do, see, take).

left_off.q: What is the past participle of 'catch'?
Why does a family of verbs fit a memory method?
left_off.a: A family shares a pattern, so one story or room holds many verbs.

story.heading: B, D, E, P, T and V sound the same

text: Picture a pilot over the sea, a controller on the ground, and a crackling radio. The pilot needs to spell the name of an airfield. She says the letters. The controller hears B, D, E, G, P, T and V, and cannot tell which is which. They all sound like the same short noise, bee, dee, ee, gee, pee, tee, vee, and an error here could be dangerous.

Radio operators had faced this since the early days of wireless. In the Second World War the Allies used a word for each letter: Able, Baker, Charlie, Dog, Easy. It worked for English speakers. But after the war, aviation became international, and a code that only works in English is not enough.

check.q: What was the problem with spoken letters on a radio?
check.a: Many letters sound alike over a noisy line, so a single letter can be mistaken for another.

parts.talk: Have you ever had to spell your name over the phone? What did you say for the difficult letters?

text: In the early 1950s the aviation authorities began to design a new alphabet. They asked linguists to help; among them was a Canadian, Jean-Paul Vinay. The new words had to be easy to say and to recognise for speakers of English, French and Spanish, with a clear and different sound for each.

They tested many words. Some were dropped because speakers of one language mispronounced them. In 1956 the final list was adopted, and it is still used today by pilots, ships, police, armies and call-centre workers: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie, Delta, Echo, Foxtrot, and on through Zulu. Two of the spellings, Alfa and Juliett, are unusual on purpose, to show French and other speakers how to say them.

check.q: What was special about the words in the final alphabet?
check.a: They were chosen to be clear and easy to recognise for speakers of English, French and Spanish.

parts.talk: Why do you think the designers asked a linguist, and not only a pilot, to help?

text: Look at the list again. It is twenty-six fixed words in a fixed order, which everyone knows, each with a picture or a sound that is easy to see. That is exactly what a memory peg is. If A is Alfa, B is Bravo, C is Charlie, you have twenty-six places in order, and you can hang any list or any set of steps on them.
So: you already know the order. All you need is a picture for each word. Then you have a second, longer set of pegs, to go with the ten body pegs, and with no building.

check.q: Why are the code words good pegs?
check.a: They are twenty-six fixed words, in a fixed order, that many people already know.

parts.talk: How many of the twenty-six words can you say now? Try the first ten.

words.m: a series of steps for doing something. The procedure for changing a tyre.
a fixed place on which you hang a picture.
a set of words used to say letters clearly on a radio or phone.
a list of things to do or to check, one by one.
to mark an item on a list as done.

source: The international spelling alphabet was finalised by the International Civil Aviation Organization in 1956. Our own account.

method.x: The code words are the pegs. Give each one a clear picture, always the same, and you can hang twenty-six things on them.

items.x: Say the code words from Alfa to Zulu until it is automatic. Singing the list can help.

items.h: Give each word one fixed picture.
items.x: Use the table, or your own: whatever you can see at once.

items.h: Turn each item you want to remember into a picture too.
items.x: Then make the item and the peg act on each other.

items.h: Recall by running through the alphabet.
items.x: Alfa, Bravo, Charlie... and see what is there.

method.title: A shopping list
method.given: Buy milk, eggs, soap, rice, in that order.
lines: A wolf milking a giant cow in the moonlight.
A crowd shouts 'Bravo!' as a giant egg is cracked open on stage.
Charlie Chaplin is washing his cane with a huge bar of soap.
A river delta is full of rice, a flood of white grains.
method.pic: Four short scenes at four pegs: a wolf and a cow, a stage and an egg, a cane and soap, a delta and rice.

method.x: Eight steps on eight pegs: A: take the wheel off. B: take out the inner tube. C: find the hole. D: dry the tube. E: put on the patch. F: check the tyre for sharp things. G: put the tube back. H: pump the tyre up. Each step is an action on its peg: an alpha-wolf removes a huge wheel; a crowd shouts 'Bravo!' at an inner tube pulled from the tyre like a snake.
Say the alphabet from Alfa to Zulu aloud, and say your picture for ten of them.

try.title: Letters and words
try.prompt: Match the letter to its code word.

try.title: A list on the pegs
try.prompt: Put these on the first five pegs: umbrella, stamps, batteries, lemon, newspaper. Write a scene for each peg.
try.model: Alfa: a wolf under a huge umbrella howling at the rain. Bravo: a crowd throws stamps at a performer, shouting bravo. Charlie: Charlie Chaplin's cane has batteries that make it jump. Delta: a delta river runs sour with lemon juice. Echo: a canyon echoes a newspaper being read aloud.
checks: Each scene has the item and the peg acting on each other.

try.title: A procedure
try.prompt: Choose a procedure with six steps (making tea, logging in, a checklist you use). Put each step on a peg A to F and write the pictures.
try.model: Making tea: A: an alpha-wolf fills a kettle. B: a crowd cheers as the water boils. C: Charlie Chaplin drops a tea bag with his cane. D: the river delta pours the water. E: an echo says 'Wait, wait, wait' as it brews. F: a fox dances with the milk.

try.q: Which is the main advantage of the alphabet pegs over a palace?
opts: No building is needed: the pegs are always in your head
try.why: They need only the twenty-six words you already know.

try.title: Spell it
try.prompt: Spell your own name and a city you know using the code words, aloud, with no mistakes.

quiz.q: What is the code word for G?
Why were the words chosen carefully?
opts: So speakers of several languages could say and hear them clearly
quiz.why: English, French and Spanish speakers all had to recognise them.

quiz.q: How many letters has the alphabet?
How do you use the pegs to recall a list?
opts: Run through Alfa to Zulu and see each picture
quiz.why: The order of the pegs gives the order of the list.

challenge.title: Memory challenge: Alfa to Mike
challenge.intro: Learn the first thirteen code words in order, with a picture for each. Type them back, one per line.
challenge.study: Say them with their pictures: wolf, crowd, cane, river delta, echo, fox...

look_back.q: Why is the past of go 'went'?
look_back.a: It is the old past of the verb 'wend', borrowed for 'go'.

look_back.q: How many body pegs are there, and what is peg 4?

look_back.a: A place on a palace route where a picture sits.

can_do: say the twenty-six code words in order.
give each a picture and use it as a peg.
put a list or a procedure on the pegs.
reflect: What procedure do you do rarely and tend to get wrong? How would you put it on the pegs?
